issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
issues.explanation: For a 56-year-old combat pilot whose index trauma is a life-threatening accident, the trigger set is dominated by bodily-state cues (dizziness, feeling ill), which fits accident-related threat. 'Other people expressing anger, even calmly' points instead toward an interpersonal/assault schema and is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, especially given the absence of other social-conflict or perpetrator-related items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies pervasive interpersonal mistrust. In this profile, the appraisals otherwise center on emotional deadness and a shattered worldview after accident trauma. Strong distrust of others is possible, but here it lacks support from the trigger/threat/memory pattern and feels mismatched with a non-interpersonal accident presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm' conflicts with the rest of the threat profile, which is strongly hypervigilant and danger-sensitive (body on alert, startle to movement) and with avoidance-based coping. While some trauma survivors do engage in risk taking, this specific item sits awkwardly in a profile otherwise organized around fear, somatic triggering, and withdrawal, without corroborating disinhibition or anger-driven strategies.

vignette: John, a 56-year-old European American combat pilot, has been struggling with symptoms following a life-threatening accident that occurred several months ago. During his routine flight training exercise, an explosion in mid-air caused severe turbulence and left him feeling dizzy and lightheaded. This traumatic event marked the beginning of his relentless battle with PTSD. John's dizziness and nausea became immediate triggers for intense anxiety, leading to a series of maladaptive strategies as he tried to regain control over his life. For example, after feeling ill one morning following a particularly vivid flashback, John decided to avoid hospitals and any medical examinations altogether. He was certain that these environments would only exacerbate his feelings of vulnerability. This avoidance behavior has extended into other areas; he no longer enjoys the activities he once loved, such as hiking and spending time with friends. The explosion sounds from fireworks on Independence Day have also triggered intense reactions. On one occasion, while driving home after a celebration, John felt dizzy and had to pull over. The unexpected movement nearby caused him to react as if he were in imminent danger. His heightened state of hypervigilance has become an almost constant presence; he finds himself constantly tense and on guard, anticipating the next potential explosion or dizziness spell. John's emotional numbness is palpable; he feels dead inside, a stark contrast to his once vibrant life. The accident shattered his beliefs about the world being safe and predictable. He now views the world as an inherently dangerous place, which has reinforced his sense of vulnerability and hypervigilance. Consequently, his maladaptive strategies have intensified. His strict control over eating is one way he tries to maintain a semblance of order in his life. The cycle of triggers, negative appraisals, threat perception, and maladaptive behaviors continues to tighten. John's emotional numbness has led him to give up activities he once found pleasurable because they no longer bring the same sense of enjoyment or relief from anxiety. He is also convinced that hospitals and medical examinations will only heighten his feelings of vulnerability, thus reinforcing his avoidance behavior. His wife notices a significant change in John's demeanor; he seems withdrawn and on edge all the time. This has strained their relationship as well as his work life. His colleagues at the base have observed a marked decline in his ability to handle high-stress situations, leading to concerns about his fitness for duty. John's maladaptive strategies have further entrenched his negative beliefs. He avoids social gatherings and medical appointments, reinforcing his emotional numbness and heightened sense of danger. The avoidance behaviors have also intensified his triggers; any sound or physical sensation that even remotely resembles the explosion now sends him into a spiral of anxiety and hypervigilance. John finally sought help after realizing that he could no longer function normally at work or in his personal life. His deepest fear is becoming entirely detached from reality, unable to engage with the world around him. He hopes for relief from his constant state of alertness and a return to feeling emotionally connected to his family and hobbies. The cycle of triggers leading to maladaptive strategies and negative appraisals has left John feeling isolated and overwhelmed. His journey towards recovery involves breaking this vicious loop, starting with understanding and addressing the specific triggers that have become so potent in his life.
